analysis.one_liner: Restores a high legal bar for government laws that burden religious practice.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by eight senators from both parties, never received a committee hearing or vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's 1990 Employment Division v. Smith decision, government no longer had to justify neutral laws that happen to block someone's religious practice. This bill would have restored a stricter rule: any federal, state, or local government restricting religious exercise would have to prove the restriction serves a compelling interest and is the least restrictive option available. It also gave people whose religion was burdened a right to sue, with attorney's fees covered.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose religious practice collides with a generally applicable law — members of minority faiths in particular, since mainstream practices rarely run into such laws. The bill defines 'person' to include religious organizations and corporations, so churches, religious schools, and religiously affiliated employers could also sue.

how_it_helps.text: Bars federal, state, and local governments from restricting a person's free exercise of religion unless the government proves the restriction is essential to a compelling interest and uses the least restrictive means.
Reverses the effect of the Supreme Court's 1990 ruling that neutral, generally applicable laws need no religious accommodation, restoring the stricter pre-1990 standard.
Gives anyone aggrieved by a violation a right to sue for relief, including against a government, and makes attorney's fees available in judicial and administrative proceedings.
Applies to existing laws and to future federal legislation unless Congress expressly exempts a statute, so the protection covers the whole body of government rules.

analysis.who_pays: Governments — federal, state, and local — would bear the burden of proving that every law or enforcement action that burdens religious practice meets the strict standard, and could face lawsuits and fee awards when they fail. Landlords, employers, and regulated parties could face religious-exemption claims under laws they otherwise must follow.

drawbacks.text: Because the bill applies to every existing and future law and defines 'person' to include corporations, it opens the door to litigation over exemptions from tax, zoning, employment, and civil-rights rules — cases where one party's religious claim imposes real costs on someone else.
Attorney's-fee provisions mean governments that lose a case pay the winning side's lawyers, adding a fiscal cost to state and local governments on top of compliance burdens.
The bill leaves the Establishment Clause untouched but does not resolve how courts should weigh a religious claimant's interest against the rights of third parties affected by an exemption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most people the bill is a straightforward civil-liberties protection: it restores a shield the Supreme Court had just removed for minority religious practices. The main cost is legal friction — more lawsuits and more exemptions carved out of uniform rules, occasionally at the expense of other people's rights or of government enforcement. Historically, a nearly identical version of this bill cleared Congress overwhelmingly and became law in 1993, so the idea had broad support; the costs were considered manageable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late October 1990 and sent to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it before the two-year Congress ended, so it died without any hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Joseph Biden introduced the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1990 on October 26, 1990, joined by seven cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Hatch and Specter and Democrats Kennedy, Inouye, Lieberman, Metzenbaum, and Moynihan.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was recorded — no hearings, markup, or floor vote — before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained or lost a legal right from this bill's death, since it never became law. Religious minorities simply remained under the Supreme Court's 1990 standard for the time being; a nearly identical bill was enacted three years later in 1993.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody — the bill simply expired in committee

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 26, 1990 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's eight sponsors split 5-3 between Democrats and Republicans, pairing ideological opposites like Kennedy and Hatch, and no opposition appears anywhere in the record; it died from inaction, not a party fight.

industries.note: The bill defines 'person' to include religious organizations, giving them a legal shield and a right to sue when government rules burden their practice. For most believers this is a protection, not a transfer of public money.
The bill adds religious-freedom claims to the list of statutes covered by federal attorney's-fee awards, expanding the pool of cases lawyers can bring and get paid for when they win.
Governments would face a strict legal test for any rule that burdens religious practice, plus litigation costs and fee awards when they lose. The cost lands partly on taxpayers.
